Connection across places: does one indicator rise where another does?

Source: R/igf.R
connassoc.Rd

For two indicators published for the same places (regions, provinces, Inuit regions), their rank correlation across places, an exact permutation p-value, and an interval that carries the sampling error of the published estimates: for connection to land and wellness, community belonging and mental health, education and health.

Usage

connassoc(
  data,
  place,
  x,
  y,
  xlo = NULL,
  xup = NULL,
  ylo = NULL,
  yup = NULL,
  reps = 10000,
  seed = 1,
  conflvl = 0.95
)

Arguments

data

A data frame, one row per place.

place

Column of place names.

x, y

Columns of the two indicators.

xlo, xup, ylo, yup

Optional columns of their published limits (for the interval).

reps

Draws for the interval and, past 8 places, for the p-value (default 10,000).

seed

Seed for the draws (default 1).

conflvl

Confidence level of rho's drawn interval (default 0.95).

Value

A list of class connassoc: data (the places used), rho, p_value, exact, rholo, rhoup, n.

Details

Mashford-Pringle and Stewart (2019) describe the land as “an instrumental part of all aspects of Indigenous life including health and well-being”; Mashford-Pringle (2016) describes Indigenous health and education as interconnected. Across places, that connection has a testable shadow: where more people are on the land (or belong, or finish school), do more report wellness? This function measures it by Spearman's \(\rho\). Its p-value is exact when there are at most 8 places (over all \(n!\) orderings) and a Monte Carlo estimate otherwise (\((b + 1)/(R + 1)\) for \(b\) of \(R\) = reps random orderings at least as extreme). Each estimate carries sampling error, so rholo and rhoup are the quantiles of \(\rho\) over reps draws of both indicators from normal distributions with their published standard errors. That is a sensitivity band, not a confidence interval for a correlation across places: it shows how much the published sampling error alone moves \(\rho\) for these places, it is pulled toward 0 (noise is added to estimates that are already noisy), and it ignores the sampling of the places themselves. Quality flags are not carried: filter suppressed rows out first.

This is an association across places (an ecological one). It cannot say that connection to land makes a person well, which needs data on persons; a handful of places gives little power; and a correlation is not a measure of the relationship the authors describe. It is a description of how the published indicators move together.

Acknowledgement

This estimator puts to quantitative use the work of Professor Angela Mashford-Pringle (Timiskaming First Nation) and Professor Suzanne Stewart (Yellowknives Dene First Nation), both of the University of Toronto.

See the acknowledgements in the section on Indigenous health of the package's vignette (vignette("crimlab")).

References

Mashford-Pringle A, Stewart SL (2019). Akiikaa (it is the land): exploring land-based experiences with university students in Ontario. Global Health Promotion 26(3_suppl):64-72. doi:10.1177/1757975919828722

Mashford-Pringle A (2016). Aboriginal health and Aboriginal education are interconnected. Research in the Sociology of Health Care 34:85-96. doi:10.1108/s0275-495920160000034005

See also

dualcont.

Examples

# your own places: made-up shares in six regions, without limits
own <- data.frame(
  region = c("North", "South", "East", "West", "Coast", "Interior"),
  language = c(41, 18, 27, 33, 22, 38),
  wellbeing = c(68, 55, 60, 66, 57, 63)
)
connassoc(own, "region", "language", "wellbeing", reps = 2000)
#> Connection across places
#> ------------------------
#> Places:           6
#> Indicators:       language and wellbeing
#> Rank correlation: rho = 0.94
#> p-value:          0.0167 (exact, every permutation)
#> 
#> Across these places the two rank strongly together.
#> 
#> An association across places only:
#> it does not show that one causes the other for any person.
